2.3.269: [Reads] ‘An if we miss to meet him handsomely—
2.3.271: Do thou so much as dig the grave for him:
2.3.272: Thou know’st our meaning. Look for thy reward
2.3.273: Among the nettles at the elder-tree
2.3.274: Which overshades the mouth of that same pit
2.3.275: Where we decreed to bury Bassianus.
2.3.276: Do this, and purchase us thy lasting friends.’
2.3.277: O Tamora! was ever heard the like?
2.3.278: This is the pit, and this the elder-tree.
2.3.279: Look, sirs, if you can find the huntsman out
2.3.280: That should have murdered Bassianus here.
2.3.281: My gracious lord, here is the bag of gold.
2.3.282: [To TITUS] Two of thy whelps, fell curs of
2.3.284: Have here bereft my brother of his life.
2.3.285: Sirs, drag them from the pit unto the prison:
2.3.286: There let them bide until we have devised
2.3.287: Some never-heard-of torturing pain for them.
2.3.288: What, are they in this pit? O wondrous thing!
2.3.290: High emperor, upon my feeble knee
2.3.291: I beg this boon, with tears not lightly shed,
2.3.292: That this fell fault of my accursed sons,
2.3.293: Accursed if the fault be proved in them,—
2.3.294: If it be proved! you see it is apparent.
2.3.295: Who found this letter? Tamora, was it you?
2.3.296: Andronicus himself did take it up.
2.3.297: I did, my lord: yet let me be their bail;
2.3.298: For, by my father’s reverend tomb, I vow
2.3.299: They shall be ready at your highness’ will
2.3.300: To answer their suspicion with their lives.
2.3.301: Thou shalt not bail them: see thou follow me.
2.3.302: Some bring the murder’d body, some the murderers:
2.3.303: Let them not speak a word; the guilt is plain;
2.3.304: For, by my soul, were there worse end than death,
2.3.305: That end upon them should be executed.
2.3.306: Andronicus, I will entreat the king;
2.3.307: Fear not thy sons; they shall do well enough.
2.3.308: Come, Lucius, come; stay not to talk with them.
2.4.1: So, now go tell, an if thy tongue can speak,
2.4.2: Who ’twas that cut thy tongue and ravish’d thee.
2.4.3: Write down thy mind, bewray thy meaning so,
2.4.4: An if thy stumps will let thee play the scribe.
2.4.5: See, how with signs and tokens she can scrowl.
2.4.6: Go home, call for sweet water, wash thy hands.
2.4.7: She hath no tongue to call, nor hands to wash;
2.4.8: And so let’s leave her to her silent walks.
2.4.9: An ’twere my case, I should go hang myself.
2.4.10: If thou hadst hands to help thee knit the cord.
2.4.11: Who is this? my niece, that flies away so fast!
2.4.12: Cousin, a word; where is your husband?
2.4.13: If I do dream, would all my wealth would wake me!
2.4.14: If I do wake, some planet strike me down,
2.4.15: That I may slumber in eternal sleep!
2.4.16: Speak, gentle niece, what stern ungentle hands
2.4.17: Have lopp’d and hew’d and made thy body bare
2.4.18: Of her two branches, those sweet ornaments,
2.4.19: Whose circling shadows kings have sought to sleep in,
2.4.20: And might not gain so great a happiness
2.4.21: As have thy love? Why dost not speak to me?
2.4.22: Alas, a crimson river of warm blood,
2.4.23: Like to a bubbling fountain stirr’d with wind,
2.4.24: Doth rise and fall between thy rosed lips,
2.4.25: Coming and going with thy honey breath.
2.4.26: But, sure, some Tereus hath deflowered thee,
2.4.27: And, lest thou shouldst detect him, cut thy tongue.
2.4.28: Ah, now thou turn’st away thy face for shame!
2.4.29: And, notwithstanding all this loss of blood,
2.4.30: As from a conduit with three issuing spouts,
2.4.31: Yet do thy cheeks look red as Titan’s face
2.4.32: Blushing to be encountered with a cloud.
2.4.33: Shall I speak for thee? shall I say ’tis so?
2.4.34: O, that I knew thy heart; and knew the beast,
2.4.35: That I might rail at him, to ease my mind!
2.4.36: Sorrow concealed, like an oven stopp’d,
2.4.37: Doth burn the heart to cinders where it is.
2.4.38: Fair Philomela, she but lost her tongue,
2.4.39: And in a tedious sampler sew’d her mind:
2.4.40: But, lovely niece, that mean is cut from thee;
2.4.41: A craftier Tereus, cousin, hast thou met,
2.4.42: And he hath cut those pretty fingers off,
2.4.43: That could have better sew’d than Philomel.
2.4.44: O, had the monster seen those lily hands
2.4.45: Tremble, like aspen-leaves, upon a lute,
2.4.46: And make the silken strings delight to kiss them,
2.4.47: He would not then have touch’d them for his life!
2.4.48: Or, had he heard the heavenly harmony
2.4.49: Which that sweet tongue hath made,
2.4.50: He would have dropp’d his knife, and fell asleep
2.4.51: As Cerberus at the Thracian poet’s feet.
2.4.52: Come, let us go, and make thy father blind;
2.4.53: For such a sight will blind a father’s eye:
2.4.54: One hour’s storm will drown the fragrant meads;
2.4.55: What will whole months of tears thy father’s eyes?
2.4.56: Do not draw back, for we will mourn with thee
2.4.57: O, could our mourning ease thy misery!
3.1.1: Hear me, grave fathers! noble tribunes, stay!
3.1.2: For pity of mine age, whose youth was spent
3.1.3: In dangerous wars, whilst you securely slept;
3.1.4: For all my blood in Rome’s great quarrel shed;
3.1.5: For all the frosty nights that I have watch’d;
3.1.6: And for these bitter tears, which now you see
3.1.7: Filling the aged wrinkles in my cheeks;
3.1.8: Be pitiful to my condemned sons,
3.1.9: Whose souls are not corrupted as ’tis thought.
3.1.10: For two and twenty sons I never wept,
3.1.11: Because they died in honour’s lofty bed.
3.1.12: For these, these, tribunes, in the dust I write
3.1.13: My heart’s deep languor and my soul’s sad tears:
3.1.14: Let my tears stanch the earth’s dry appetite;
3.1.15: My sons’ sweet blood will make it shame and blush.
3.1.16: O earth, I will befriend thee more with rain,
3.1.17: That shall distil from these two ancient urns,
3.1.18: Than youthful April shall with all his showers:
3.1.19: In summer’s drought I’ll drop upon thee still;
3.1.20: In winter with warm tears I’ll melt the snow
3.1.21: And keep eternal spring-time on thy face,
3.1.22: So thou refuse to drink my dear sons’ blood.
3.1.23: O reverend tribunes! O gentle, aged men!
3.1.24: Unbind my sons, reverse the doom of death;
3.1.25: And let me say, that never wept before,
3.1.26: My tears are now prevailing orators.
3.1.27: O noble father, you lament in vain:
3.1.28: The tribunes hear you not; no man is by;
3.1.29: And you recount your sorrows to a stone.
3.1.30: Ah, Lucius, for thy brothers let me plead.
3.1.31: Grave tribunes, once more I entreat of you,—
3.1.32: My gracious lord, no tribune hears you speak.
3.1.33: Why, tis no matter, man; if they did hear,
3.1.34: They would not mark me, or if they did mark,
3.1.35: They would not pity me, yet plead I must;
3.1.36: Therefore I tell my sorrows to the stones;
3.1.37: Who, though they cannot answer my distress,
3.1.38: Yet in some sort they are better than the tribunes,
3.1.39: For that they will not intercept my tale:
3.1.40: When I do weep, they humbly at my feet
3.1.41: Receive my tears and seem to weep with me;
3.1.42: And, were they but attired in grave weeds,
3.1.43: Rome could afford no tribune like to these.
3.1.44: A stone is soft as wax,—tribunes more hard than stones;
3.1.45: A stone is silent, and offendeth not,
3.1.46: And tribunes with their tongues doom men to death.
3.1.47: But wherefore stand’st thou with thy weapon drawn?
3.1.48: To rescue my two brothers from their death:
3.1.49: For which attempt the judges have pronounced
3.1.51: O happy man! they have befriended thee.
3.1.52: Why, foolish Lucius, dost thou not perceive
3.1.53: That Rome is but a wilderness of tigers?
3.1.54: Tigers must prey, and Rome affords no prey
3.1.55: But me and mine: how happy art thou, then,
3.1.56: From these devourers to be banished!
3.1.57: But who comes with our brother Marcus here?
3.1.58: Titus, prepare thy aged eyes to weep;
3.1.59: Or, if not so, thy noble heart to break:
3.1.60: I bring consuming sorrow to thine age.
3.1.61: Will it consume me? let me see it, then.
3.1.64: Ay me, this object kills me!
3.1.65: Faint-hearted boy, arise, and look upon her.
3.1.67: Hath made thee handless in thy father’s sight?
3.1.68: What fool hath added water to the sea,
3.1.69: Or brought a faggot to bright-burning Troy?
3.1.70: My grief was at the height before thou camest,
3.1.71: And now like Nilus, it disdaineth bounds.
3.1.72: Give me a sword, I’ll chop off my hands too;
3.1.73: For they have fought for Rome, and all in vain;
3.1.74: And they have nursed this woe, in feeding life;
3.1.75: In bootless prayer have they been held up,
3.1.76: And they have served me to effectless use:
3.1.77: Now all the service I require of them
3.1.78: Is that the one will help to cut the other.
3.1.79: ’Tis well, Lavinia, that thou hast no hands;
3.1.80: For hands, to do Rome service, are but vain.
3.1.81: Speak, gentle sister, who hath martyr’d thee?
3.1.82: O, that delightful engine of her thoughts
3.1.83: That blabb’d them with such pleasing eloquence,
3.1.84: Is torn from forth that pretty hollow cage,
3.1.85: Where, like a sweet melodious bird, it sung
3.1.86: Sweet varied notes, enchanting every ear!
3.1.87: O, say thou for her, who hath done this deed?
3.1.88: O, thus I found her, straying in the park,
3.1.89: Seeking to hide herself, as doth the deer
3.1.90: That hath received some unrecuring wound.
3.1.91: It was my deer; and he that wounded her
3.1.92: Hath hurt me more than had he killed me dead:
3.1.93: For now I stand as one upon a rock
3.1.94: Environed with a wilderness of sea,
3.1.95: Who marks the waxing tide grow wave by wave,
3.1.96: Expecting ever when some envious surge
3.1.97: Will in his brinish bowels swallow him.
3.1.98: This way to death my wretched sons are gone;
3.1.99: Here stands my other son, a banished man,
3.1.100: And here my brother, weeping at my woes.
3.1.101: But that which gives my soul the greatest spurn,
3.1.102: Is dear Lavinia, dearer than my soul.
3.1.103: Had I but seen thy picture in this plight,
3.1.104: It would have madded me: what shall I do
3.1.105: Now I behold thy lively body so?
3.1.106: Thou hast no hands, to wipe away thy tears:
3.1.107: Nor tongue, to tell me who hath martyr’d thee:
3.1.108: Thy husband he is dead: and for his death
3.1.109: Thy brothers are condemn’d, and dead by this.
3.1.110: Look, Marcus! ah, son Lucius, look on her!
3.1.111: When I did name her brothers, then fresh tears
3.1.112: Stood on her cheeks, as doth the honey-dew
3.1.113: Upon a gather’d lily almost wither’d.
3.1.114: Perchance she weeps because they kill’d her husband;
3.1.115: Perchance because she knows them innocent.
3.1.116: If they did kill thy husband, then be joyful
3.1.117: Because the law hath ta’en revenge on them.
3.1.118: No, no, they would not do so foul a deed;
3.1.119: Witness the sorrow that their sister makes.
3.1.120: Gentle Lavinia, let me kiss thy lips.
3.1.121: Or make some sign how I may do thee ease:
3.1.122: Shall thy good uncle, and thy brother Lucius,
3.1.123: And thou, and I, sit round about some fountain,
3.1.124: Looking all downwards to behold our cheeks
3.1.125: How they are stain’d, as meadows, yet not dry,
3.1.126: With miry slime left on them by a flood?
3.1.127: And in the fountain shall we gaze so long
3.1.128: Till the fresh taste be taken from that clearness,
3.1.129: And made a brine-pit with our bitter tears?
3.1.130: Or shall we cut away our hands, like thine?
3.1.131: Or shall we bite our tongues, and in dumb shows
3.1.132: Pass the remainder of our hateful days?
3.1.133: What shall we do? let us, that have our tongues,
3.1.134: Plot some deuce of further misery,
3.1.135: To make us wonder’d at in time to come.
3.1.136: Sweet father, cease your tears; for, at your grief,
3.1.137: See how my wretched sister sobs and weeps.
3.1.138: Patience, dear niece. Good Titus, dry thine eyes.
3.1.139: Ah, Marcus, Marcus! brother, well I wot
3.1.140: Thy napkin cannot drink a tear of mine,
3.1.141: For thou, poor man, hast drown’d it with thine own.
3.1.142: Ah, my Lavinia, I will wipe thy cheeks.
3.1.143: Mark, Marcus, mark! I understand her signs:
3.1.144: Had she a tongue to speak, now would she say
3.1.145: That to her brother which I said to thee:
3.1.146: His napkin, with his true tears all bewet,
3.1.147: Can do no service on her sorrowful cheeks.
3.1.148: O, what a sympathy of woe is this,
3.1.149: As far from help as Limbo is from bliss!
3.1.150: Titus Andronicus, my lord the emperor
3.1.151: Sends thee this word,—that, if thou love thy sons,
3.1.152: Let Marcus, Lucius, or thyself, old Titus,
3.1.153: Or any one of you, chop off your hand,
3.1.154: And send it to the king: he for the same
3.1.155: Will send thee hither both thy sons alive;
3.1.156: And that shall be the ransom for their fault.
3.1.157: O gracious emperor! O gentle Aaron!
3.1.158: Did ever raven sing so like a lark,
3.1.159: That gives sweet tidings of the sun’s uprise?
3.1.160: With all my heart, I’ll send the emperor My hand:
3.1.161: Good Aaron, wilt thou help to chop it off?
3.1.162: Stay, father! for that noble hand of thine,
3.1.163: That hath thrown down so many enemies,
3.1.164: Shall not be sent: my hand will serve the turn:
3.1.165: My youth can better spare my blood than you;
3.1.166: And therefore mine shall save my brothers’ lives.
3.1.167: Which of your hands hath not defended Rome,
3.1.168: And rear’d aloft the bloody battle-axe,
3.1.169: Writing destruction on the enemy’s castle?
3.1.170: O, none of both but are of high desert:
3.1.171: My hand hath been but idle; let it serve
3.1.172: To ransom my two nephews from their death;
3.1.173: Then have I kept it to a worthy end.
3.1.174: Nay, come, agree whose hand shall go along,
3.1.175: For fear they die before their pardon come.
3.1.177: By heaven, it shall not go!
3.1.178: Sirs, strive no more: such wither’d herbs as these
3.1.179: Are meet for plucking up, and therefore mine.
3.1.180: Sweet father, if I shall be thought thy son,
3.1.181: Let me redeem my brothers both from death.
3.1.182: And, for our father’s sake and mother’s care,
3.1.183: Now let me show a brother’s love to thee.
3.1.184: Agree between you; I will spare my hand.
3.1.185: Then I’ll go fetch an axe.
3.1.186: But I will use the axe.
3.1.187: Come hither, Aaron; I’ll deceive them both:
3.1.188: Lend me thy hand, and I will give thee mine.
3.1.189: [Aside] If that be call’d deceit, I will be honest,
3.1.190: And never, whilst I live, deceive men so:
3.1.191: But I’ll deceive you in another sort,
3.1.192: And that you’ll say, ere half an hour pass.
3.1.193: Now stay your strife: what shall be is dispatch’d.
3.1.194: Good Aaron, give his majesty my hand:
3.1.195: Tell him it was a hand that warded him
3.1.196: From thousand dangers; bid him bury it
3.1.197: More hath it merited; that let it have.
3.1.198: As for my sons, say I account of them
3.1.199: As jewels purchased at an easy price;
3.1.200: And yet dear too, because I bought mine own.
3.1.201: I go, Andronicus: and for thy hand
3.1.202: Look by and by to have thy sons with thee.
3.1.203: Their heads, I mean. O, how this villany
3.1.204: Doth fat me with the very thoughts of it!
3.1.205: Let fools do good, and fair men call for grace.
3.1.206: Aaron will have his soul black like his face.
3.1.207: O, here I lift this one hand up to heaven,
3.1.208: And bow this feeble ruin to the earth:
3.1.209: If any power pities wretched tears,
3.1.211: What, wilt thou kneel with me?
3.1.212: Do, then, dear heart; for heaven shall hear our prayers;
3.1.213: Or with our sighs we’ll breathe the welkin dim,
3.1.214: And stain the sun with fog, as sometime clouds
3.1.215: When they do hug him in their melting bosoms.
3.1.217: And do not break into these deep extremes.
3.1.218: Is not my sorrow deep, having no bottom?
3.1.219: Then be my passions bottomless with them.
3.1.220: But yet let reason govern thy lament.
3.1.221: If there were reason for these miseries,
3.1.222: Then into limits could I bind my woes:
3.1.223: When heaven doth weep, doth not the earth o’erflow?
3.1.224: If the winds rage, doth not the sea wax mad,
3.1.225: Threatening the welkin with his big-swoln face?
3.1.226: And wilt thou have a reason for this coil?
3.1.227: I am the sea; hark, how her sighs do blow!
3.1.228: She is the weeping welkin, I the earth:
3.1.229: Then must my sea be moved with her sighs;
3.1.230: Then must my earth with her continual tears
3.1.231: Become a deluge, overflow’d and drown’d;
3.1.232: For why my bowels cannot hide her woes,
3.1.233: But like a drunkard must I vomit them.
3.1.234: Then give me leave, for losers will have leave
3.1.235: To ease their stomachs with their bitter tongues.
3.1.236: Worthy Andronicus, ill art thou repaid
3.1.237: For that good hand thou sent’st the emperor.
3.1.238: Here are the heads of thy two noble sons;
3.1.239: And here’s thy hand, in scorn to thee sent back;
3.1.240: Thy griefs their sports, thy resolution mock’d;
3.1.241: That woe is me to think upon thy woes
3.1.242: More than remembrance of my father’s death.
3.1.243: Now let hot AEtna cool in Sicily,
3.1.244: And be my heart an ever-burning hell!
3.1.245: These miseries are more than may be borne.
3.1.246: To weep with them that weep doth ease some deal;
3.1.247: But sorrow flouted at is double death.
3.1.248: Ah, that this sight should make so deep a wound,
3.1.249: And yet detested life not shrink thereat!
3.1.250: That ever death should let life bear his name,
3.1.251: Where life hath no more interest but to breathe!
3.1.252: Alas, poor heart, that kiss is comfortless
3.1.253: As frozen water to a starved snake.
3.1.254: When will this fearful slumber have an end?
3.1.256: Thou dost not slumber: see, thy two sons’ heads,
3.1.257: Thy warlike hand, thy mangled daughter here:
3.1.258: Thy other banish’d son, with this dear sight
3.1.259: Struck pale and bloodless; and thy brother, I,
3.1.260: Even like a stony image, cold and numb.
3.1.261: Ah, now no more will I control thy griefs:
3.1.262: Rend off thy silver hair, thy other hand
3.1.263: Gnawing with thy teeth; and be this dismal sight
3.1.264: The closing up of our most wretched eyes;
3.1.265: Now is a time to storm; why art thou still?
3.1.267: Why dost thou laugh? it fits not with this hour.
3.1.268: Why, I have not another tear to shed:
3.1.269: Besides, this sorrow is an enemy,
3.1.270: And would usurp upon my watery eyes
3.1.271: And make them blind with tributary tears:
3.1.272: Then which way shall I find Revenge’s cave?
3.1.273: For these two heads do seem to speak to me,
3.1.274: And threat me I shall never come to bliss
3.1.275: Till all these mischiefs be return’d again
3.1.276: Even in their throats that have committed them.
3.1.277: Come, let me see what task I have to do.
3.1.278: You heavy people, circle me about,
3.1.279: That I may turn me to each one of you,
3.1.280: And swear unto my soul to right your wrongs.
3.1.281: The vow is made. Come, brother, take a head;
3.1.282: And in this hand the other I will bear.
3.1.283: Lavinia, thou shalt be employ’d: these arms!
3.1.284: Bear thou my hand, sweet wench, between thy teeth.
3.1.285: As for thee, boy, go get thee from my sight;
3.1.286: Thou art an exile, and thou must not stay:
3.1.287: Hie to the Goths, and raise an army there:
3.1.288: And, if you love me, as I think you do,
3.1.289: Let’s kiss and part, for we have much to do.
3.1.291: The wofull’st man that ever lived in Rome:
3.1.292: Farewell, proud Rome; till Lucius come again,
3.1.293: He leaves his pledges dearer than his life:
3.1.295: O, would thou wert as thou tofore hast been!
3.1.296: But now nor Lucius nor Lavinia lives
3.1.297: But in oblivion and hateful griefs.
3.1.298: If Lucius live, he will requite your wrongs;
3.1.299: And make proud Saturnine and his empress
3.1.300: Beg at the gates, like Tarquin and his queen.
3.1.301: Now will I to the Goths, and raise a power,
3.1.302: To be revenged on Rome and Saturnine.
3.2.1: So, so; now sit: and look you eat no more
3.2.2: Than will preserve just so much strength in us
3.2.3: As will revenge these bitter woes of ours.
3.2.5: Thy niece and I, poor creatures, want our hands,
3.2.6: And cannot passionate our tenfold grief
3.2.7: With folded arms. This poor right hand of mine
3.2.8: Is left to tyrannize upon my breast;
3.2.9: Who, when my heart, all mad with misery,
3.2.10: Beats in this hollow prison of my flesh,
3.2.11: Then thus I thump it down.
3.2.12: Thou map of woe, that thus dost talk in signs!
3.2.13: When thy poor heart beats with outrageous beating,
3.2.14: Thou canst not strike it thus to make it still.
3.2.15: Wound it with sighing, girl, kill it with groans;
3.2.16: Or get some little knife between thy teeth,
3.2.17: And just against thy heart make thou a hole;
3.2.18: That all the tears that thy poor eyes let fall
3.2.19: May run into that sink, and soaking in
3.2.20: Drown the lamenting fool in sea-salt tears.
3.2.21: Fie, brother, fie! teach her not thus to lay
3.2.22: Such violent hands upon her tender life.
3.2.23: How now! has sorrow made thee dote already?
3.2.24: Why, Marcus, no man should be mad but I.
3.2.25: What violent hands can she lay on her life?
3.2.26: Ah, wherefore dost thou urge the name of hands;
3.2.27: To bid AEneas tell the tale twice o’er,
3.2.28: How Troy was burnt and he made miserable?
3.2.29: O, handle not the theme, to talk of hands,
3.2.30: Lest we remember still that we have none.
3.2.31: Fie, fie, how franticly I square my talk,
3.2.32: As if we should forget we had no hands,
3.2.33: If Marcus did not name the word of hands!
3.2.34: Come, let’s fall to; and, gentle girl, eat this:
3.2.35: Here is no drink! Hark, Marcus, what she says;
3.2.36: I can interpret all her martyr’d signs;
3.2.37: She says she drinks no other drink but tears,
